source_text: Sit ergo nostri operis exordium quaestio illa consequens ac secunda, utrum potestate unius dei mundus regatur anne multorum. nemo, qui quidem sapiat rationemque secum putet, non unum esse intellegat, qui et condiderit omnia et eadem qua condidit uirtute moderetur. quid enim multis opus est ad mundi regimen sustinendum? nisi forte arbitrabimur, si plures sint, minus habere singulos neruorum atque uirium: quod quidem faciunt ii qui esse multos uolunt, quia necesse est inbecillos esse, siquidem singuli sine auxilio reliquorum tantae molis gubernaculum sustinere non possunt. deus autem, qui est aeterna mens, ex omni utique parte perfectae consummataeque uirtutis est: quod si uerum est, unus sit necesse est. potestas enim uel uirtus absoluta retinet suam propriam firmitatem. id autem solidum existimandum est, cui nihil decedere, id perfectum, cui nihil possit accedere. quis dubitet potentissimum esse regem qui totius orbis habeat imperium? neque inmerito. cum illius sint Quae ubique sunt omnia cum ad eum solum omnes undique copiae congerantur. at si plures partiantur orbem, minus certe opum, minus uiriuni singuli habebunt, cum intra praescriptam portionem se quisque contineat. eodem modo etiam dii, si plures sint, minus ualebunt, aliis tantundem in se habentibus. uirtutis autem perfecta natura in eo potest esse in quo totum est quam in eo in quo pars exigua de toto est. deus uero si perfectus est, ut esse debet, non potest esse nisi unus, ut in eo sint omnia. deorum igitur uirtutes ac potestates infirmiores sint necesse est, quia tantum singulis deerit, quantum in ceteris fuerit: ita quanto plures tanto minores erunt. quid quod summa illa rerum potestas ac diuina uis ne semel quidem diuidi potest? quidquid enim capit diuisionem, et interitum capiat necesse est. si autem interitus procul est a deo, quia incorruptibilis est et aeternus, consequens est ut diuidi potestas diuina non possit. deus ergo unus est, si nihil esse aliut potest quod : tantundem capiat potestatis: et ii tamen qui multos esse arbitrantur officia inter se dicunt esse partitos. de quibus omnibus suo loco disputabimus. illud interim quod ad praesentem locum pertinet teneo: si partiti sunt inter se officia, eodem reuoluitur res, ut ex iis quilibet sufficere omnibus nequeat. perfectus igitur non erit qui cessantibus ceteris non potest omnia gubernare. ita fit ut ad regendum mundum unius perfecta uirtute opus sit quam inbecillitate multorum. qui autem putat hanc tantam magnitudinem non posse ab uno regi, fallitur neque quanta sit uis ac potestas diuinae maiestatis intellegit, si existimat singularem deum qui facere mundum potuit, eundem regere non posse quem fecit. at si concipiat animo quanta sit diuini huius operis inmensitas (eamque) cum antea nihil esset, tamen uirtute atque consilio dei ex nihilo esse conflatam, quod opus nisi ab uno inchoari perficique non potuit, iam intelleget multo facilius esse ab uno regi quod est ab uno constitutum. dicat fortasse aliquis ne tabricari quidem tam inmensum opus mundi nisi a pluribus potuisse. quamlibet multos, quamlibet magnos faciat, quidquid in multis magnitudinis potestatis uirtutis maiestatisque posuerit, id totum in unum confero et in uno esse dico, ut tantum in eo sit istarum rerum, quantum nec cogitari nec dici potest. qua in re quoniam et sensu deficimur et uerbis, quia neque tantam intellegentiae lucem pectus humanum neque explanationem tantarum rerum capit lingua mortalis, id ipsum intellegere nos oportet ac dicere. uideo rursus quid e contrario dici possit, tales esse illos plures qualem nos uolumus unum. at hoc fieri nullo pacto potest, quod singulorum potestas progredi longius non ualebit occurrentibus sibi potestatibus ceterorum. necesse est enim ut suos quisque limites aut transgredi nequeat aut si transgressus fuerit, suis alterum finibus pellat. non uident qui deos multos esse credunt fieri posse ut aliquid diuersum uelint, ex qua re disceptatio inter eos et certamen oriatur; sicut Homerus bellantes inter se deos finxit, cum alii Troiam capi uellent, alii repugnarent. unius igitur arbitrio mundum regi necesse est. nisi enim singularum partium potestas ad unam prouidentiam referatur, non poterit summa ipsa constare, uno quoque nihil curante amplius quam quod ad eum proprie pertinet, sicut ne res quidem militaris nisi unum habeat ducem atque rectorem. quodsi in uno exercitu tot fuerint imperatores quot legiones, quot cohortes, quot cunei, quot alae, primum nec instrui poterit acies uno quoque periculum recusante nec regi facile aut temperari, quod suis propriis consiliis utantur omnes, quorum diuersitate plus noceant quam prosint: sic in hoc rerum naturae imperio nisi unus fuerit ad quem totius summae cura referatur, uniuersa soluentur et conruent. dicere autem multorum arbitrio regi mundum tale est, quale si quis adfirmet in uno corpore multas esse mentes, quoniam multa et uaria sint ministeria membrorum, ut singulos corporis sensus singulae mentes regere credantur, item multi adfectus, quibus commoueri solemus uel ad iram uel ad cupiditatem uel ad laetitiam uel ad metum uel ad miserationem, ut in his omnibus totidem mentes putentur operari. quod si quis profecto dicat, ne ipsam quidem quae una est habere uideatur. quodsi in uno corpore tantarum rerum gubernationem mens una possidet et uniuersis simul intenta est, cur aliquis existimet mundum non posse ab uno regi, a pluribus posse? quod quia intellegunt isti adsertores deorum, ita eos praeesse singulis rebus ac partibus dicunt, ut tamen unus sit rector eximius. iam ergo ceteri non dii erunt, sed satellites ac ministri, quos ille unus maximus ac potens omnium iis officiis praefecerit, ut ipsi eius imperio ac nutibus seruiant. si uniuersi pares non sunt, non igitur dii omnes sunt: nec enim potest hoc idem esse quod seruit et quod dominatur. nam si deus nomen est summae potestatis, incorruptibilis esse debet, perfectus inpassibilis nulli rei subiectus. ergo dii non sunt quos parere um maximo deo necessitas cogit. sed quia non frustra falluntur qui hoc ita putant, causam huius erroris paulo post aperiemus. nunc unitatem diuinae potestatis testimoniis conprobemus.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore let the beginning of our work be that question which follows and is second, whether the world is ruled by the power of one God or of many. No one, who indeed is wise and considers reason with himself, does not understand that there is one who both founded all things and governs them with the same virtue with which he founded them. For what need is there for many for sustaining the rule of the world? Unless perhaps we might think that if there are more, individual ones have less nerve and strength: which indeed those who want there to be many do, because it is necessary for them to be weak, since individual ones cannot sustain the helm of such a great burden without the help of the rest. But God, who is eternal mind, is perfect and complete virtue in every part: which if it is true, it is necessary for there to be one. For absolute power or virtue retains its own firmness. That which is solid is to be considered as having nothing lacking, that which is perfect is to be considered as having nothing that can be added to it. Who would doubt that the king who has the command of the whole world is most powerful? And not without reason. For all things that are everywhere are his, and all resources from everywhere are gathered to him alone. But if many divide the world, individual ones will certainly have less wealth, less strength, since each one is contained within his prescribed portion. In the same way also, if there are many gods, they will be less strong, having as much in themselves as others have. The perfect nature of virtue can be in that in which the whole is, rather than in that in which a small part of the whole is. But if God is perfect, as he ought to be, he cannot be anything except one, so that all things may be in him. Therefore the virtues and powers of the gods must be weaker, because as much is lacking to individual ones as is in the others: thus the more there are, the smaller they will be. What about the fact that the highest power of things and divine strength cannot even once be divided? For whatever undergoes division must also undergo destruction. But if destruction is far from God, because he is incorruptible and eternal, it follows that divine power cannot be divided. Therefore God is one, if nothing else can have as much power: and yet those who think there are many say that they have divided offices among themselves. We will dispute about all these things in their own place. Meanwhile, I hold to what pertains to the present place: if they have divided offices among themselves, the matter returns to the same thing, so that each one cannot suffice for all things. Therefore he will not be perfect who cannot govern all things when the others are absent. Thus it happens that for ruling the world, the perfect virtue of one is needed rather than the weakness of many. But he who thinks that this great magnitude cannot be ruled by one is mistaken and does not understand how great the strength and power of divine majesty is, if he thinks that the singular God who could make the world cannot rule what he made. But if he conceives in his mind how great the immensity of this divine work is (and that) with nothing previously existing, nevertheless it was made from nothing by the virtue and counsel of God, which work could not have been begun and completed except by one, then he will understand that it is much easier for it to be ruled by one than it was to be established by one. Perhaps someone will say that not even a work as immense as the world could have been made by fewer than many. Whatever multitude, whatever greatness he may make, whatever magnitude of power, virtue, and majesty he may place in many, I confer all that upon one and say that it exists in one, so that there is as much of those things in him as cannot be thought or said. In this matter, since we fail both in sense and in words, because the human breast does not grasp such great light of understanding, nor does the mortal tongue grasp the explanation of such great things, we ought to understand and say this very thing. I see again what can be said to the contrary, that those many are such as we want the one to be. But this cannot happen in any way, because the power of individual ones will not be able to proceed further, with the powers of the others occurring to them. For it is necessary that each one have his own limits, which he cannot transgress, or if he has transgressed, he drives another back with his own boundaries. Those who believe that there are many gods do not see that it is possible for them to will something different, from which a dispute and contest arise among them; just as Homer fashioned the gods fighting among themselves, when some wanted Troy to be taken, and others resisted. Therefore it is necessary for the world to be ruled by the decision of one. For unless the power of individual parts is referred to one providence, the sum itself will not be able to exist, with each one caring for nothing more than what pertains to him, just as not even a military thing can have more than one leader and ruler. But if in one army there are as many commanders as there are legions, cohorts, wedges, and wings, first the battle line will not be able to be drawn up, with each one refusing his own danger, nor will it be easy to rule or temper, because all use their own counsel, whose diversity harms more than it helps: thus in this command of nature, unless there is one to whom the care of the whole sum is referred, all things will be dissolved and will collapse. But to say that the world is ruled by the decision of many is such as if someone were to affirm that in one body there are many minds, because there are many and varied ministries of the members, so that individual minds are believed to rule individual senses of the body, and also many affections, by which we are moved either to anger or to desire or to joy or to fear or to pity, so that in all these things as many minds as there are are thought to operate. Which if someone were to say, not even the one that is alone is seen to have. But if in one body one mind possesses the governance of so many things and is attentive to all things at the same time, why would anyone think that the world cannot be ruled by one, but can be ruled by many? Because those who assert the gods understand this, they say that they preside over individual things and parts, so that nevertheless there is one excellent ruler. Now therefore the others will not be gods, but satellites and ministers, whom that one greatest and most powerful of all has placed over those offices, so that they serve his command and nods. If all are not equal, therefore not all are gods: for it cannot be the same thing that serves and that dominates. For if God is the name of the highest power, it ought to be incorruptible, perfect, impassible, subject to no thing. Therefore those are not gods whom necessity compels to obey the greatest God. But because those who think this are not mistaken in vain, we will reveal the cause of this error a little later. Now we will confirm the unity of divine power with testimonies.

choices.why: to maintain the unity of divine power
to explain the diversity of the world
to emphasize God's ability to rule the world
to provide evidence for the unity of divine power

pass_b_english: So let our work begin with the second question that follows: whether the world is ruled by the power of one God or of many. No one who is wise and consults reason fails to see that there is one who both founded all things and governs them with the same virtue by which he founded them. What need is there for many to sustain the rule of the world? One might suppose that if there are several, each has less nerve and strength; but those who want many gods do so because it is necessary for them to be weak, since no single one can bear the helm of so great a burden without the help of the rest. God, however, who is eternal mind, is perfect and complete virtue in every respect. If that is true, there must be one. Absolute power or virtue retains its own firmness. What is solid lacks nothing; what is perfect admits nothing further. Who would doubt that the king who holds command of the whole world is most powerful? And not without reason: all things everywhere are his, and all resources from every quarter are gathered to him alone. But if many divide the world, each will certainly have less wealth and less strength, since each is confined to his allotted portion. The same holds for gods: if there are many, they will be weaker, because each has no more in himself than the others have. Perfect virtue can reside only in that which contains the whole, not in that which contains a mere part. If God is perfect, as he must be, he cannot be anything but one, so that all things may be in him. Therefore the virtues and powers of the gods must be inferior, for each lacks exactly as much as resides in the others: the more there are, the smaller they become. The supreme power of things and divine strength cannot be divided even once. Whatever undergoes division must also undergo destruction. But destruction is far from God, because he is incorruptible and eternal; therefore divine power cannot be divided. God is one, if nothing else can possess as much power. Yet those who think there are many say they have divided offices among themselves. We will dispute all these points in their proper place. For now I hold to what belongs to the present argument: if they have divided offices, the matter returns to the same point, so that no one of them can suffice for all things. He will not be perfect who cannot govern all things when the others are absent. Thus ruling the world requires the perfect virtue of one, not the weakness of many. Whoever thinks this great magnitude cannot be ruled by one is mistaken and does not understand how great the strength and power of divine majesty is, if he supposes that the singular God who could make the world cannot rule what he made. But if he conceives in his mind how great the immensity of this divine work is—how, when nothing previously existed, it was brought into being from nothing by the virtue and counsel of God, a work that could not have been begun and completed except by one—he will then understand that it is far easier for it to be ruled by one than it was to be established by one. Someone may say that not even so immense a work as the world could have been made without many. Let him imagine whatever multitude, whatever greatness, whatever magnitude of power, virtue, and majesty he pleases in many; I gather it all into one and say it exists in one, so that there is as much of those things in him as cannot be thought or spoken. In this matter we fail both in sense and in words, because the human heart cannot grasp such great light of understanding, nor can mortal tongue grasp the explanation of such great things; yet we ought to understand and say this very thing. I see again what might be said on the contrary: that those many are such as we want the one to be. But this cannot happen in any way, because the power of each will not be able to advance further when met by the powers of the others. Each must have his own limits, which he cannot cross, or if he crosses them he drives another back with his own boundaries. Those who believe in many gods do not see that it is possible for them to will something different, from which a dispute and contest would arise among them, just as Homer fashioned gods fighting among themselves when some wanted Troy taken and others resisted. Therefore the world must be ruled by the decision of one. Unless the power of individual parts is referred to one providence, the whole itself cannot hold together, each caring for nothing more than what belongs to him—just as even a military force cannot have more than one leader and ruler. If in one army there were as many commanders as legions, cohorts, wedges, and wings, first the battle line could not be formed, each refusing his own danger, nor would it be easy to rule or temper, because all would follow their own counsels, whose diversity harms more than it helps. So in this command of nature, unless there is one to whom the care of the whole sum is referred, all things will dissolve and collapse. To say that the world is ruled by the decision of many is like affirming that in one body there are many minds, because there are many and varied ministries of the members, so that individual minds are believed to rule individual senses of the body, and also many affections by which we are moved—to anger, desire, joy, fear, pity—so that as many minds are thought to operate. If someone said that, he would not even be seen to have the one mind that is alone. But if in one body one mind possesses the governance of so many things and is attentive to all at once, why would anyone think the world cannot be ruled by one but can be ruled by many? Because those who assert the gods understand this, they say the gods preside over individual things and parts, yet there is one excellent ruler. Now therefore the others would not be gods but satellites and ministers, whom that one greatest and most powerful of all has placed over those offices to serve his command and nods. If all are not equal, then not all are gods: it cannot be the same thing that serves and that dominates. If God is the name of the highest power, he must be incorruptible, perfect, impassible, subject to nothing. Therefore those whom necessity compels to obey the greatest God are not gods. But because those who think this are not mistaken in vain, we will reveal the cause of this error a little later. Now we will confirm the unity of divine power with testimonies.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of Lactantius's argument regarding the necessity of a single ruler for the universe. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Latin source. All clauses, including the complex analogies of the military and the human body, are preserved. Scripture/literary references (Homer) are correctly handled.

The translation accurately reflects the Latin text, preserving the argumentation, theological concepts, and logical structure. The title 'God's Unity' appropriately captures the central theme. The translation maintains the original meaning, including the distinction between one God and many gods, the nature of divine power, and the argument for the unity of divine governance. The scriptural citations are not present in the Latin text, and the translation does not add any. The translation is faithful to the source, with no omissions or additions that alter the meaning. The translation is complete and accurate, with no errors in the representation of the Latin text.
